name: car+cdr
summary: Takes a pair apart into its head and its tail in one call, returning both as multiple values.
explanation: car+cdr is (values (car p) (cdr p)) with a name. It exists because taking a pair apart is one conceptual act and writing it as two calls forces you to name the pair, mention it twice, and hope both mentions stay in sync. With multiple values the decomposition is a single expression, and call-with-values or let-values binds both halves at once. That matters most inside a recursion, where the pair being destructured is often itself an expression rather than a variable -- with car and cdr you must let-bind it first or evaluate it twice. The verb is not faster; the engine still does the same two field reads. What it buys is that the head and the tail arrive together, which is the shape every list-consuming loop actually wants. Because it returns multiple values it cannot be used where a single value is expected: it must be received, not embedded. That is the one thing that surprises people, and it is the same rule that governs every values-returning verb in the language.

examples.note: (1 (2 3)) -- the head and the tail arrive as two separate values, received by a two-argument lambda.
(three (1 (2 3)) one (9 ()) nested ((a b) (c))) -- a one-element list gives an empty tail, and the head keeps whatever structure it had.

examples.code:
(define (sum-list xs)
  (if (null? xs)
      0
      (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs))
                        (lambda (head tail) (+ head (sum-list tail))))))
(display (list (sum-list '(1 2 3 4)) (sum-list '()) (sum-list '(7))))
(newline)
examples.note: (10 0 7) -- the recursion names head and tail once each, which is the shape car+cdr is for.

caveats: It returns TWO values, not a pair or a list. Writing (list (car+cdr xs)) does not give you what you expect; the result has to be received by call-with-values or let-values.
It raises on the empty list, exactly as car does. car+cdr is not a safe destructure -- check null? first.
It is not faster than calling car and cdr separately. The gain is that the pair is mentioned once, which matters when the pair is an expression rather than a variable.
It works on any pair, not only on proper lists. (car+cdr '(1 . 2)) gives 1 and 2, and the second value is not a list.
The value order is head then tail, matching the name. Receiving them the other way round type-checks fine and silently computes nonsense.
usecases: Destructuring the pair at the head of a recursion without let-binding it or evaluating it twice.
Writing a loop that consumes a list one element at a time and needs both the element and the remainder in scope.
Feeding both halves of a pair into a two-argument procedure in one step.

learn.concept: Multiple values let one call answer a question that has two parts, without inventing a container to hold them.
learn.progression: Write a recursion with car and cdr and count how many times the list is mentioned. Rewrite it with car+cdr and count again. Then try to use the result as if it were a list, watch it not work, and you have learned what multiple values actually are.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (peel-command tokens)
  (if (null? tokens)
      (list 'verb 'none 'args '())
      (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr tokens))
                        (lambda (verb args) (list 'verb verb 'args args)))))
(display (list (peel-command '(move north quickly)) (peel-command '(quit)) (peel-command '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (head-and-rest-sum xs)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs))
                    (lambda (first rest) (list 'first first 'rest-sum (apply + rest) 'total (+ first (apply + rest))))))
(display (list (head-and-rest-sum '(10 1 2 3)) (head-and-rest-sum '(5))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define improper '(1 . 2))
(display (list 'proper (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr '(1 2))) list)
               'dotted (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr improper)) list)
               'tail-is-list (list? (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr '(1 2))) (lambda (h t) t)))
               'dotted-tail-is-list (list? (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr improper)) (lambda (h t) t)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A command parser has to split an input into its verb and its arguments. Candidates: car+cdr (one call, both halves named at once, and it reads as the single act it is), car and cdr separately (identical result, but the token list is mentioned twice and must be a variable or it gets evaluated twice), match or a destructuring macro (Motoi has none -- this is the language's destructuring), split-at with index 1 (works, allocates, and returns the head wrapped in a one-element list you then have to unwrap), pattern-matching on length first (a whole extra traversal to learn something car+cdr's null? guard already covers). car+cdr wins on readability, not speed.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: peeling a verb off a command line, with the empty case handled before the destructure because car+cdr will not do it for you. math: taking the head off and summing the rest, showing that the two halves reconstitute the whole. cs: the pair-versus-list distinction -- car+cdr works on a dotted pair and the tail it hands back is then not a list, which is a fact a caller that assumed proper input would discover late.
row-2-audit.meta: Why car+cdr and not car plus cdr: on a variable they are equivalent and the separate calls are arguably clearer. The verb earns itself when the pair is a subexpression, because then the alternative is either a let or a double evaluation.
row-2-audit.eng: Verb-and-arguments is the shape of every command line and every message dispatch. Getting both in one step is why the parser stays four lines.
row-2-audit.math: A non-empty sequence is exactly its head paired with its tail; the decomposition is total on non-empty input and undefined on empty, which is why the guard comes first.
row-2-audit.cs: car+cdr is defined on pairs, not on lists. If the tail might not be a list, the code downstream has to say so -- the destructure will not raise, it will just hand you something surprising.

row-3-dimension.setup: Splitting one thing into its first part and everything else, and getting hold of both at the same moment.

rungs.domain: a stream of millisecond timestamps, separating the moment that just happened from the ones still queued
rungs.code:
(define (next-event queue)
  (if (null? queue)
      (list 'idle)
      (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr queue))
                        (lambda (now later)
                          (list 'at-ms now 'pending (length later)
                                'gap-ms (if (null? later) 0 (- (car later) now)))))))
(display (list (next-event '(100 140 210)) (next-event '(500)) (next-event '())))
(newline)

rungs.domain: an interpreter reading an application form into its operator and its operands
rungs.code:
(define (analyse form)
  (if (not (pair? form))
      (list 'atom form)
      (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr form))
                        (lambda (operator operands)
                          (list 'apply operator 'arity (length operands)
                                'nested (length (filter pair? operands)))))))
(display (list (analyse '(+ 1 (* 2 3) 4)) (analyse '(quit)) (analyse 'x)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: Structurally it is one pair pulled apart, and the only interesting case is the one-element list whose tail is empty. On a timestamp queue the head becomes NOW and the tail becomes LATER, and having both in hand at once is what makes the gap to the next event computable in the same expression -- with two separate calls the queue is mentioned three times. In an interpreter the head becomes the operator and the tail becomes the operands, which is the exact moment a list stops being data and becomes a call; the arity and the nesting both fall out of the tail. Same destructure every time. What climbs is what the two halves MEAN: nothing, then now-versus-later, then operator-versus-operands.
row-3-dimension.meta: The third rung is why this verb is in a list library rather than a utility drawer. Reading a form as operator-plus-operands is the first step of every evaluator ever written, and it is precisely a car+cdr.
row-3-dimension.eng: An event loop always wants the current event and the remaining queue together. Fetching them separately is where an off-by-one between 'what I am handling' and 'what is left' gets in.
row-3-dimension.math: Head-and-tail is the initial algebra of lists: every non-empty list is uniquely a cons of one element onto another list, which is why structural recursion over lists always terminates.
row-3-dimension.cs: Operator and operands is the shape of application. Once a form is destructured that way the evaluator's remaining job is entirely about the operands.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (rebuilds-the-pair? xs)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs))
                    (lambda (head tail) (equal? (cons head tail) xs))))
(display (map rebuilds-the-pair?
              (list '(1) '(1 2) '(1 2 3) '((a) b) '(1 . 2))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (halves-agree-with-accessors? xs)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs))
                    (lambda (head tail) (and (equal? head (car xs)) (equal? tail (cdr xs))))))
(display (map halves-agree-with-accessors?
              (list '(0) '(1 2) '(a b c) '(#f #f) '((x . y) z))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (tail-is-one-shorter? xs)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs))
                    (lambda (head tail) (= (length tail) (- (length xs) 1)))))
(display (map tail-is-one-shorter?
              (list '(1) '(1 2) '(1 2 3 4) '(()) '(a b c d e))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: Consing the two returned values back together reproduces the original pair exactly; each value equals what the corresponding accessor would have returned; and on a proper list the tail is always exactly one element shorter than the input.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all pairs p. cons(car+cdr(p)) = p; head = car(p) and tail = cdr(p); and for all non-empty proper lists xs. |tail| = |xs| - 1
row-4-proof.meta: The first claim is the strong one: it is an equivalence, saying the decomposition loses nothing and cons is its exact inverse. The second is the compatibility claim against the accessors it replaces, and the third pins the list-specific consequence. What would falsify them: a swapped value order (the first two both fail), a copied rather than shared tail (all three still pass -- which is why sharing is a caveat and not a proof here), or an off-by-one in a list-based implementation. The dotted pair in the first program is deliberate: the round-trip law holds for every pair, not only for proper lists, and the length law in the third program does not, which is why they are separate claims.
row-4-proof.eng: Round-tripping through cons is the test that says a destructure is lossless. Anything weaker only tests that it returned something.
row-4-proof.math: cons and car+cdr are mutually inverse on the set of pairs -- an isomorphism between pairs and ordered pairs of values. That is the formal content of 'a pair holds exactly two things'.
row-4-proof.cs: The length law is what makes structural recursion terminate: every step hands the recursion something strictly smaller, and the empty list is the floor.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (peel xs) (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs)) list))
(define (run-pipeline stages input)
  (let loop ((remaining stages) (value input) (trace '()))
    (if (null? remaining)
        (list 'result value 'trace (reverse trace))
        (let ((split (peel remaining)))
          (let ((stage (car split)) (rest (cadr split)))
            (loop rest (stage value) (cons value trace)))))))
(display (run-pipeline (list (lambda (n) (* n 2)) (lambda (n) (+ n 1)) (lambda (n) (* n n))) 3))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (decompose xs) (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr xs)) list))
(define (running-max xs)
  (if (null? xs)
      '()
      (let ((d (decompose xs)))
        (let loop ((rest (cadr d)) (best (car d)) (out (list (car d))))
          (if (null? rest)
              (reverse out)
              (let ((d2 (decompose rest)))
                (let ((next (max best (car d2))))
                  (loop (cadr d2) next (cons next out)))))))))
(display (running-max '(3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (split-form form) (call-with-values (lambda () (car+cdr form)) list))
(define (depth form)
  (if (not (pair? form))
      0
      (let ((d (split-form form)))
        (+ 1 (apply max 0 (map depth (cons (car d) (cadr d))))))))
(display (list 'flat (depth '(a b c))
               'nested (depth '(a (b (c d)) e))
               'atom (depth 'x)
               'deep (depth '(((((x)))))))) 
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: car+cdr hands back the head and the tail of a pair together.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: peel is one call; run-pipeline uses it to walk a list of stage procedures, applying each to the value and recording the trace -- the list of functions is consumed by the same destructure that a list of numbers would be, because a procedure is just another element. math: decompose is one call; running-max carries the best-so-far through the tail and emits it at every step, turning a fold into a scan. cs: split-form is one call; depth recurses into BOTH halves and takes the max, which measures how deeply nested an s-expression is -- a tree walk written entirely in terms of the pair decomposition.
row-5-emergence.meta: All three are the same skeleton: destructure, do something with the head, recur on the tail. The cs one departs by recursing on the head as WELL, which is the moment a list walk becomes a tree walk -- and the only change is one extra call in the recursive position. That is the whole distance between a list and a tree.
row-5-emergence.eng: A pipeline is a fold over functions. Once you see that the stage list destructures exactly like a data list, the special-purpose pipeline runner stops being special-purpose.
row-5-emergence.math: A scan keeps every intermediate of a fold. Running maximum is monotone by construction, so the output is a non-decreasing sequence regardless of the input.
row-5-emergence.cs: Recursing on the car as well as the cdr is the difference between iteration and tree traversal, and it is the reason s-expressions can represent programs at all.
